subject: Communication
title: Agenda Setting: What Media Tells You to Think About
description: A quick, practical guide to Agenda Setting: What Media Tells You to Think About.

hook.text: Media may not tell you what to think. But it's remarkably good at telling you what to think about.

buildup.text: McCombs and Shaw's agenda-setting theory: the issues media covers most become the issues the public considers most.

discovery.text: If a news channel covers crime 24/7, viewers believe crime is rising — even when statistics show it's falling.

twist.text: What media doesn't cover matters equally. Issues absent from coverage become invisible to public consciousness.

climax.text: Media literacy means asking: 'Who decided this was news? What's being covered — and what's being ignored?'

punchline.text: The news doesn't show you the world. It shows you a selection of it.

quiz.question: What does agenda-setting theory describe?
options: Media tells people what to think
Media influences what people think about by choosing coverage topics

details.summary: Agenda-setting theory, developed by McCombs and Shaw in 1972, shows that media may not tell you what to think but powerfully determines what you think about. By choosing which stories to cover and how prominently, media shapes public priorities and perceived reality.
details.whyItMatters: Agenda-setting reveals that the most important media power is the power of selection. What is omitted matters as much as what is covered.
takeaways: Media determines which issues the public considers important
Story selection and prominence shape perceived reality
What media leaves out is as influential as what it covers

faq.question: How does agenda-setting differ from media bias?
faq.answer: Media bias is about how a story is told, while agenda-setting is about which stories get told at all. A news outlet can cover a story accurately but still exercise enormous power by choosing to cover it prominently while ignoring other important stories entirely.

faq.question: Who sets the media's agenda?
faq.answer: Multiple forces compete: political elites provide stories, PR firms pitch narratives, audience metrics reward certain topics, advertisers influence coverage indirectly, and editors make daily choices about prominence. The resulting agenda emerges from this complex interaction of interests.
